query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used at high temperatures, the suppression of atomic clustering—and thereby the preservation of a uniform single-phase structure—is governed by a low atomic size mismatch among constituent elements, which minimizes local strain and inhibits chemical segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly mixed high-entropy nanoalloy (e.g., a variant of Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni) with a baseline composition exhibiting moderate atomic size differences.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the atomic size mismatch by substituting one minor element with an alternative element of significantly different atomic radius while keeping overall composition and processing conditions constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature annealing (e.g., 800–1000 °C) under an inert atmosphere to simulate operational conditions in high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering and potential nanoscale interfacial segregation that arises from differences in local strain due to atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: In nanoalloys with lower atomic size mismatch, reduced local strain limits the driving force for atomic clustering; in contrast, larger mismatches increase local distortions, promoting clustering and emergent phase separations that compromise structural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoalloys engineered with minimal atomic size mismatch will exhibit significantly lower degrees of clustering and maintain a stable, single-phase structure under high-temperature conditions relative to those with higher mismatch, as observed via XRD, electron microscopy, and atom-probe tomography.
generation.baseline: The baseline alloy (with moderate atomic size differences) is expected to show some degree of short-range clustering when annealed at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This prediction is bounded to high-temperature regimes (approximately 800–1000 °C) in inert atmospheres; deviations may occur with significant changes in alloy chemistry, processing history, or the presence of additional stabilizing mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold at which atomic size mismatch becomes critical in driving clustering, as well as the possible interplay with other factors such as surface/interface energy and entropy contributions, remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy nanoalloy samples with the same overall composition but with systematic variations in atomic size mismatch (through targeted substitution). Anneal all samples at 800–1000 °C in an inert atmosphere and then characterize phase uniformity and degree of atomic clustering using X-ray diffraction (for phase identification), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography.
measurements: Phase composition via XRD to detect phase separation or emergence of secondary phases
Grain and cluster size distributions via high-resolution TEM
Atomic-scale clustering quantified by pair correlation functions in atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with lower atomic size mismatch do not show a statistically significant reduction in clustering or secondary phase formation compared to alloys with higher mismatch, or if the degree of clustering is equivalent or greater, then the hypothesis is falsified.

(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. High Entropy Alloys Mined From Binary Phase Diagrams

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are a new type of high-performance structural material. Their vast degrees of compositional freedom provide for extensive opportunities to design alloys with tailored properties. However, compositional complexities present challenges for alloy design. Current approaches have shown limited reliability in accounting for the compositional regions of single solid solution and composite phases. For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented. The hypothesis is that the HEA structural stability is encoded within the phase diagrams. Accordingly, we introduce several phase-diagram inspired parameters and employ machine learning (ML) to classify 600+ reported HEAs based on these parameters. Compared to other large database statistical prediction models, this model gives more detailed and accurate phase predictions. Both the overall HEA prediction and specifically single-phase HEA prediction rate are above 80%.
